title: We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs
gist: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are spreading fast (11% of Americans using them for weight loss vs 3% in 2024) and Eli Lilly/Novo Nordisk data link them to 2-3 years younger biological age, but side-effect evidence is still emerging (GI issues, pancreatitis, contested vision-loss lawsuits, hair and nail effects), and the WHO advises against drug treatment for obesity in children under 10 despite a 310-fold rise in US prescriptions for 8-11-year-olds.

insights.claim: According to Gallup, 11% of Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024, and 15% say they have used one for weight loss at some point.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Rapid GLP-1 adoption supports the Eli Lilly/Novo Nordisk growth thesis and second-order effects on food and health sectors.
insights.locator: And a lot of people are taking them.

insights.claim: Findings from Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk show overweight and diabetic people on GLP-1s have a biological age about two to three years younger than similar individuals on placebo, fueling framing of GLP-1s as longevity drugs.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: A longevity label could expand the addressable market and pricing narrative for GLP-1 makers.
insights.locator: This week my colleague Antonio Regalado

insights.claim: Beyond approved uses in diabetes, chronic kidney disease and obesity, GLP-1s are being researched for substance-use disorders, neurodegenerative disease and cancer.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Indication expansion is a major optionality driver for GLP-1 franchises.

insights.claim: Dozens of people are suing Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly claiming GLP-1 drugs caused an optic nerve condition that can lead to sudden vision loss; both companies dispute the claims and research on the link is mixed.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Product-liability litigation is a tail risk for GLP-1 makers.
insights.locator: Some claim that, in rare cases

insights.claim: Electronic health data from 67 US health-care organizations associated GLP-1 use with increased hair-loss risk, though it is not thought to be common, and a small study found 66% of users reported a nail disorder, also common among non-users.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Emerging side-effect signals could affect adherence and label warnings but appear modest.

insights.claim: Between 2019 and 2026 there was a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for US children aged eight to 11 with obesity, though child prescriptions remain rare.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Pediatric use is a growing but scrutinized market segment.
insights.locator: The side effects might look different in children

insights.claim: The WHO's first guidelines on child and adolescent obesity explicitly do not recommend pharmacological treatment for kids under 10, citing lack of evidence on benefits and adverse effects on growth and development, despite an estimated 70 million obese children aged five to nine in 2024.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: WHO caution could slow pediatric GLP-1 uptake and influence regulators and payers outside the US.

insights.claim: The volume of GLP-1 research is vast, with probably hundreds of studies underway, so the side-effect picture will keep evolving.
insights.speaker: Jessica Hamzelou
insights.so_what: Ongoing evidence flow means continued headline risk, positive and negative, for GLP-1 makers.
